questions.question: How do you create a custom exception in Java?
options: Using the `new Exception` keyword directly in the code
By extending the Exception or RuntimeException class
By declaring it as a static final constant
explanations: new Exception only creates an instance, it does not define a new type.
Correct. To create a custom exception you define a class that inherits from Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked).
Exception is a class, not an interface; it cannot be implemented.
Constants do not define new exception types.

questions.question: Why is it useful to create custom exceptions?
options: To make the code faster at runtime
To represent errors specific to the application's domain
To avoid using try-catch in the code
explanations: Custom exceptions do not improve code performance.

Correct. Custom exceptions allow you to represent errors that are specific to the application's context (e.g. InsufficientBalanceException, UserNotFoundException), making the code more expressive and maintainable.
They do not replace standard exceptions; they complement them.

questions.question: Which constructors should a custom exception typically have?
options: Only an empty constructor without parameters
A constructor with an error message and optionally a cause
A constructor that receives an Error object
explanations: An empty constructor is useful, but not enough for a complete custom exception.
Correct. The typical approach is to have a constructor that accepts an error message (String message) and optionally a cause (Throwable cause) for exception chaining.
It is not necessary to have 10 parameters; the common constructors are message and cause.
The constructor does not receive an Error object; it inherits from Exception.

questions.question: When is it better to create a checked exception vs a custom unchecked exception?
options: Always use checked exceptions for every kind of error
Checked if the caller can recover from the error; unchecked if it is a programming error
Always use unchecked exceptions because they are easier to use
It depends on the size of the file where the exception is defined
explanations: Not every kind of error should be checked; it depends on the context.

Correct. A checked exception is used when the error is recoverable and the caller must handle it (e.g. file not found). An unchecked exception is used when it is a programming error that should be fixed (e.g. null argument).
Unchecked is not always the best option; the context must be evaluated.
The size of the file does not determine the type of exception.
